description:
THE MERGE-POLICY APPROVAL FLOW EARNS ITS FRICTION BACK. Asked for by the operator 2026-09-10, the same day the `review` zones were DISARMED across the fleet: every `review` rule in two downstream repositories' `.chief/zones.conf` became `serialize`, each file carrying a dated DISARMED banner saying why. The hold was costing more than it caught.

THE DEFECT IS GRANULARITY, NOT THE HOLD. A path-glob zone cannot tell 'added a routine adapter under a watched path' from 'changed the policy that path guards'. `zones_match` keys on `path:<glob>` against each changed file and on `touches:<domain>` as an exact tag — both are FILE-LEVEL or COARSER, so every branch that brushed a watched directory held, every hold read as noise, AND EVERY HOLD WAS APPROVED UNREAD. An approval nobody reads is worse than no approval, because it manufactures a record of review that did not happen.

WHAT IS NOT LOST, AND MUST NOT BE TOUCHED. The merge floor is untouched by the disarm and by this work: rebase onto the latest base, re-verify, merge `--no-ff` still catches textual interference and staleness. What is lost until this lands is the HUMAN CHECKPOINT ON DESIGN-LEVEL OVERLAP — two branches whose code is individually correct and whose designs disagree, which is where a person has standing and a test does not. Do not weaken the floor to buy granularity, and do not turn chief into a conflict resolver: 'No AI auto-conflict-resolution' stays true.

RE-ARMING MUST STAY A ONE-WORD EDIT. Today re-arming is `serialize` -> `review` per rule, and that property is worth keeping: a repo that disarmed should be able to re-arm without rewriting its registry. If a finer rule needs new syntax, the OLD SYNTAX MUST KEEP WORKING with its current meaning, and the new form must be opt-in.

THE MECHANISM TO REUSE, NEVER TO DUPLICATE. `zones_merge_gate` is the merge phase's one 'green is not enough authority' question, and `budget_holds` already shows how a second rule joins it: it contributes zone-shaped hold lines into the same match, so there is ONE checksum, ONE request file, ONE `chief approve`, whether a branch tripped a declared zone, an oversized story, or both at once. That no-double-prompting property is load-bearing. The surrounding pieces are `zones_digest` (a cksum over the sorted changed-file list plus the sorted matched zones, which BINDS an approval to exactly what it approved so a later change re-asks), `zones_write_request` / `zones_approved` / `zones_record_approval`, `zones_render`, `zones_show`, `zones_approve`, and `zones_clear_record`, which deletes the approval file on merge.

MEASURE THE FRICTION RATHER THAN ASSERTING IT. The claim being fixed is that holds were noise. Prove the new rule is better by running it against real history: how many of the holds that actually fired would still fire, and how many of the changes the operator would have wanted held still hold. A rule that holds nothing is not an improvement over a rule that holds everything — both get ignored. Report both directions.

KEEP IT OUT OF THE WORKER BODY. The quality ratchet counts raw line span and the merge phase already sits inside a very long function. New logic belongs in its own engine module, sourced the way `budget.sh` and `zones.sh` are, with a line in CLAUDE.md's layout.

NOT IN SCOPE: the resolution-deletion hold, which is its own tasklist and its own always-armed rule. This tasklist changes how holds are TARGETED and PRESENTED; it does not remove any existing hold.

userStories.title: A zone can say what within a path is load-bearing, and the old syntax keeps its meaning
acceptanceCriteria: The registry gains a way to distinguish a change to a watched surface from a change merely underneath a watched path. The chosen mechanism is stated in the notes with the alternatives that were rejected and why, and it is evaluated against the existing matcher set rather than bolted beside it — `zones_match` stays the one place a rule is evaluated.

BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY IS PINNED BY TEST: an existing `.chief/zones.conf` using only `path:<glob>` and `touches:<domain>` behaves exactly as it does today, `review` and `serialize` unchanged, and re-arming a disarmed rule stays a one-word `serialize` -> `review` edit. A test asserts both, and a test asserts a repo with NO zones.conf still behaves exactly as it did before the feature existed — the property `test/overlap-zones.sh` PART A already guards.

A malformed or unknown line is reported on stderr and IGNORED, never fatal — the existing rule that a registry typo never takes down a run. A test drives the new syntax misspelled and asserts the run completes with the rule skipped and reported.

The matcher is evaluated with the same NOGLOB discipline the current splitter uses, so a pattern survives word splitting as a literal and is never expanded against the worktree. A test pins a pattern that would expand if the guard were dropped.
`shellcheck -S error` and `bash -n` are clean on every changed script.
GATES: `bash -n` + `shellcheck -S error` clean; `test/{smoke,ratelimit,noworkguard}.sh` green; `VERSION` bumped (`test/version-bump.sh`); `ROADMAP.md` names this stem (`test/doc-sync.sh`).

userStories.title: The hold says what it is asking about, precisely enough to be read
acceptanceCriteria: A hold names the specific surface that triggered it and what about the branch touched it — not merely the glob that matched and the first file that hit it. The same detail reaches all four places a hold is reported today: the worker log, the approval request file, the run summary's awaiting-approval block, and `chief approve --list`. A long list is truncated with a count, never silently.

The single-prompt property is preserved and proven: a branch that trips a declared zone AND an oversized story under a blocking diff budget still produces ONE checksum, ONE request file and ONE `chief approve`. A test drives both at once and asserts exactly one prompt.

The approval stays bound by checksum to exactly what it approved, so a re-push that changes the branch re-asks. A test changes the branch after approval and asserts the hold returns. The existing digest's inputs are updated only if the new rule changes what is being approved, and the notes justify any change to them.

Existing behaviour is preserved end to end: `test/overlap-zones.sh` stays green across PART A (a serialize zone is a no-op at merge), PART B (a review zone holds a rebased, GREEN branch and the scheduler is NOT blocked — the sibling still merges in the same run), PART C (the verdict survives a restart and an in-flight approval lands without a second run), PART D (the diff budget under warn and under block) and PART E (stale records are not actionable). Any fixture that had to change is named in the notes with the reason, and a fixture is never loosened to make a new rule pass.

`awaiting-approval` remains the state, `chief approve <name> -m <reason>` remains the override, and no new park state and no new approval command are introduced. A test asserts the state name and the command surface are unchanged.
GATES: `bash -n` + `shellcheck -S error` clean; `test/{smoke,ratelimit,noworkguard}.sh` green; `VERSION` bumped (`test/version-bump.sh`); `ROADMAP.md` names this stem (`test/doc-sync.sh`).

userStories.title: The friction is measured against real history, in both directions
acceptanceCriteria: The new rule is run against recorded merge history and the result is reported BOTH ways: how many historically-fired holds would still fire under it, and how many would now pass unheld. The notes record the corpus that was measured (how many merges, over what span), the counts, and at least one concrete example from each direction. The measurement is read-only — it inspects history and changes nothing.

The result is judged rather than merely reported: the notes state whether the rule earns its friction, and if the measurement says it does not, what was changed in response. A rule that holds nothing gets ignored exactly like a rule that holds everything, and the notes address that directly.

A hermetic test drives the real driver with a scripted fake agent in a temp repo and proves the distinction the whole tasklist exists for: a branch that only adds a routine consumer under a watched path MERGES unheld, and a branch that changes the watched surface itself is HELD with the surface named. Both run against the same registry, and the notes record the observed output of each.

The test is mutation-checked: with the new discrimination neutered in a COPY of the engine (not `git show HEAD~N`, because CI clones shallow), the first branch is held again — so the test is shown to reproduce the defect rather than restate behaviour that always worked.
Any new test file is added to all three gate lists: `.chief/verify.sh`'s bystander tests, `test/all.sh`'s suite, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which must still parse.
New logic lives in its own engine module sourced by the driver rather than added to the worker body, and CLAUDE.md's layout has a line for it. The quality ratchet stays green.

`docs/reference/overlap-zones.md` documents the new rule under its banner: the syntax, the backward-compatible meaning of the old forms, the one-word re-arm, and the rule's LIMIT — it targets holds more precisely, it does not judge whether a design is right. `ROADMAP.md`'s Planned row is updated from `(proposed — no tasklist authored yet)` to name this stem, and states that re-arming a disarmed registry is now a one-word edit per rule that a repo can make when it chooses. The disarmed repositories are referred to by role; this repo is public and names no downstream repository.

GATES: `bash -n` + `shellcheck -S error` clean; `test/{smoke,ratelimit,noworkguard}.sh` and `test/overlap-zones.sh` green; `bash test/doc-sync.sh` green; `VERSION` bumped (`test/version-bump.sh`); `chief lint` clean.
